newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.African rand slides as forex D-Day looms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.African rand slides as forex D-Day looms.

text.p: The South African rand fell to a five-month low on Monday as banks stocked up on dollars ahead of a milestone relaxation of foreign exchange controls from July 1.

But the country's financial markets remained generally upbeat, despite the weaker currency and a fall in the gold price. Most analysts expect the relaxation of controls to occur without triggering a big capital flight or a run on the rand.

Individual South Africans will be allowed to invest 200,000 rand ($44,000) offshore from Tuesday, the first time they have been able to export capital since the imposition of current exchange control regulations in 1961.
At the 1400 GMT local close, the rand was trading at 4.5280/5310 against the dollar, its lowest level since February 5, from 4.5145/5175 late on Friday.

The markets have been nervous of the move, fearing a wholesale exodus of capital from the country. But concerns have been soothed by the central Reserve Bank's buildup of reserves and credit lines of some 38 billion rand which it has said it can access to smooth possible market volatility.
Dealers said the currency had held up pretty well in the face of the easing of capital controls.
"If you look at the rand at 4.53 it is not bad at all. It has performed very well considering the exchange control move," one foreign exchange trader said.

The Reserve Bank predicts that the measure will spark outflows of three to five billion rand. Some economists put it slightly higher, but few expect outflows to exceed 10 billion rand in the coming months.

With official foreign reserves standing at a record 21.8 billion rand at May 31 and expected to have increased further in June, traders are sanguine the central bank has the ammunition to smooth any short-term currency shocks.
As a result, the markets are looking beyond the easing of capital controls to an expected interest rate cut, possibly around September.

Rate cut hopes have been fuelled by a better-than-expected fall in the annual consumer inflation rate to 9.5 percent in May from 9.9 percent in April, coupled with a decline in both M3 money supply and private credit extension last month.
The expectation of cheaper credit continued to propel the Johannesburg Stock Exchange on Monday, where both the industrial and all-share indices climbed to new record highs.
Bullion's slide to its weakest level in over four years winded South African gold shares, cutting three percent off the index at the close.
But industrial stocks turned a blind eye to gold's woes, surging to new peaks, helped by interest rate optimism and quarter-end demand from unit trusts.
